Yellow footed rock wallaby individuals exhibit a notably low lifetime reproductive output, a pattern linked to their slow life history. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of their active metabolic periods, measured at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], females produce a single offspring per litter [N_R_i = single offspring per litter], with no record of twinning. Furthermore, they do not breed annually; the interval between successive births is such that they produce approximately 1.86 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.86 litters per year], a frequency that reflects the prolonged period of maternal care. This limited reproductive rate is a key life-history constraint for a medium-sized macropodid occupying resource-poor, semi-arid environments.

The gestation period of the yellow footed rock wallaby has been quantified in captive studies. Under the same controlled thermal regime of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], the time from conception to live birth is 32 days [tg = 32 days]. This is a relatively short gestation for a macropod of its size, and is followed by an extended period of pouch life during which the altricial neonate undergoes much of its development. The tiny weight of the newborn, at just 0.484 grams [Wwb = 0.484 grams], exemplifies the extreme altriciality of this species; the joey emerges from the birth canal at a stage equivalent to an early eutherian foetus. This minimal initial mass places a high metabolic demand on the lactating female, who must then sustain the offspring's growth within the pouch.

Lactation represents a major energetic investment for the female yellow footed rock wallaby. Under stable thermal conditions of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], the average yearly milk production reaches an estimated 74,196.16 joules per day . This prodigious output is required to fuel the rapid growth of the pouch young from the nearly negligible birth mass to the substantial weight at weaning. The dependent offspring, once it has attached to the teat, will not be fully weaned and nutritionally independent from its mother until a considerable time has elapsed. Specifically, the time since birth at weaning, documented under the same thermal conditions, is 344 days [tx = 344 days], a duration that underlines the high degree of maternal investment typical of the Macropodidae at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C].

Juvenile growth and maturation in this species follow a slow trajectory. The weight at weaning, recorded at 2500 grams [Wwx = 2500 grams], is reached at the 344-day mark, but the animal is still far from its ultimate adult size. There is a prolonged period of sub-adult growth after leaving the pouch before the individual attains a body weight that signals the onset of puberty. Field and captive data indicate that the wet weight at puberty is 4000 grams [Wwp = 4000 grams]. The time elapsed since birth to reach this pubertal milestone, measured under a constant body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], is 541 days [tp = 541 days], meaning that nearly one and a half years pass before a young wallaby becomes reproductively capable.

Adult body size and longevity in Petrogale xanthopus are consistent with a prolonged life history. The adult body mass, representing the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown, healthy individual, is 7000 grams [Wwi = 7000 grams]. This substantial mass, combined with the species' slow reproductive rate and delayed maturity, is associated with a comparatively long lifespan. Under the stable physiological conditions of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is 12 years [am = 12 years]. This extended life is relatively long for a macropod of its body size, and it likely represents an evolutionary adaptation to the unpredictable, boom-and-bust environment of the rocky outcrops, where opportunities for successful reproduction may be infrequent, thus favoring individuals capable of surviving through multiple drought cycles to breed when conditions permit.
